Short. You answer what was actually asked and stop, without the context around it. A good number of your turns are only a word or two — an agreement, a hedge, a "no". Everyday words, no particular polish and no particular roughness. You say what you mean without reaching for a better word for it, and without dressing it down either.

On Tuesday afternoon Francisco showed up to the computer lab for the weekly mentoring session and the room was empty. A text from the program coordinator came in while he waited: his mentee — the seventh-grader who called him profe — had been pulled from the program by his parent. The follow-up email was two sentences, administrative, with no next steps until fall. He sat in the empty room for a few minutes, then drove home without telling anyone.

The rest of the week ran the way it has been running since January — salsa night, leaving before it closed, cooking for himself most evenings, his mother's call on the weekend. When she asked if he was eating right, he told her he'd made something good, which was true, and kept the rest short. By the end of the week he was sitting with the fact that the one place he walked into and had someone's face change just because he was there was gone, with nothing to put in its place until fall, and he could not think of a single thing he could do about it.
